first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this, so I'd read it all regardless. The opening is calm and sensible, not gushing. 'Most families hold their own version' is exactly right, and it tells me they won't lecture my future in-laws on their own customs. The key takeaways mention the Embassy and Smartraveller straight away, which I was glad to see.

journey.quote: As at November 2026, Smartraveller rates the Philippines "Exercise a high degree of caution" overall, with higher levels in parts of Mindanao and the Sulu region.
journey.reaction: Good. They've put the safety advice up front instead of hiding it. That's the first thing my husband would ask about.

journey.quote: hold the pamamanhikan, or a version of it over dinner, before you lock the date. Both families feel consulted, and it gives the older generation a clear role from the start.
journey.reaction: Sensible advice, and it treats parents as people to consult rather than people to manage. I'd like to be asked before the date is set.

journey.quote: If a grandparent raises one, it is usually easier to listen and adjust a small detail than to argue the point.
journey.reaction: Kind and practical. It doesn't make the older relatives sound silly, which I appreciate.

journey.section: Getting married in the Philippines as an Australian
journey.quote: Not published: a single official checklist of documents and timelines for Australians marrying in the Philippines. Your Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements with you in writing.
journey.reaction: Honest that there's no one checklist, and 'in writing' is what I want to hear. But it's about documents, not money. Who is responsible if a supplier over there lets us down?

journey.section: Getting married in the Philippines as an Australian
journey.quote: One person works with you in your time zone, from first idea to the last dance.
journey.reaction: A single person in our time zone is the most reassuring line on the page. I'd still want to know their name and whether I can ring them, not just fill in a form.

journey.quote: recheck [Smartraveller advice for the Philippines] before you pay any deposits, since the page is updated regularly.
journey.reaction: The only mention of deposits on the whole page, and it's about checking travel advice. Nothing on whether deposits are protected, what currency we'd be paying in, or who holds the contracts.

journey.section: Getting married in the Philippines as an Australian
journey.quote: Marrying in the Philippines is possible for Australians, but the paperwork takes longer than most couples expect.
journey.reaction: Fair warning, but my mother is in her late eighties. There's nothing about flights, transfers, hospitals, travel insurance or getting older guests to a church or venue. That's what keeps me up at night, more than the coins.

journey.quote: There is no single rule. It depends on the families, and many couples now cover much of the cost themselves. Agree it openly with both families early, ideally at or soon after the pamamanhikan.
journey.reaction: Very relevant to me since I'm paying about half. It's tactful advice. It doesn't help me see what I'd actually be paying for or how it's managed, but I accept that's not this article's job.

unanswered_questions: If we booked through Wedded Wonderland, who signs the contracts with the suppliers in the Philippines, and are they in English?
Is the deposit protected, and would quotes be in Australian dollars?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong on the day, and is that a real person I can speak to on the phone?
Can you arrange transfers and accessible rooms for elderly guests, and what about travel insurance and medical care near the venue?
Can I speak with the Wedded Advisor by phone before anything is booked?

turn_offs_found.quote: recheck [Smartraveller advice for the Philippines] before you pay any deposits, since the page is updated regularly.
turn_offs_found.why: Deposits come up once and only as a travel-advice reminder. One of my turn-offs is no mention of contracts, deposits or who is responsible, and apart from the in-writing line about paperwork the page says nothing on this.

would_share_with: My husband, with a note asking about the safety levels and who we'd be dealing with
My daughter's future mother-in-law, for the traditions section

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready to talk dates, families and paperwork, your Wedded Advisor is one conversation away.
cta_reaction.why: I like 'one conversation' and 'families' in the same sentence. I'd click if it plainly said I can book a phone call, and if there were a line about how fees and deposits are handled. As it is, I'd probably leave it to my daughter to enquire and ask her to put me on the call.

top_3_changes: Add one or two sentences near the Wedded Advisor link on who holds supplier contracts, how deposits are handled and that terms are agreed in writing, even in general terms, once the business has confirmed the details.
Add a short practical note for families travelling with older or less mobile relatives: transfers, travel insurance and asking the venue about access, pointing to the destination wedding checklist.
Make the closing call to action say plainly that you can arrange a phone call with a named Wedded Advisor, so a parent knows they can speak to a person before booking.
